Historically, this chapter is read within the following setting: The narrative belongs to Genesis's primeval history. Its event chronology and literary formation are debated, so the entry distinguishes the narrated world from the dates of surviving Mesopotamian flood witnesses.
Historically, this chapter is read within the following setting: Genesis presents Abraham as the ancestor through whom Israel traces its identity, land promise, and blessing to the nations.

Historically, this chapter is read within the following setting: Abraham stands in the ancestral narratives of Genesis as the father of the covenant line. His story reflects clan migration, land promise, and divine promise in an early biblical setting rather than a fixed modern chronology.
Historically, this chapter is read within the following setting: Passover stands at the center of the exodus tradition and the formation of Israel as a redeemed people.
